# Project 3: INS/GNSS Integration {#sec-project3}

When the Boeing 747 entered service in 1970 it carried three Delco Carousel inertial navigators, each drifting on the order of a nautical mile per hour, and crossing an ocean meant comparing the three with each other and with whatever radio fix the crew could get. Today a receiver the size of a fingernail hands you a fix every second, and the inertial sensor in your pocket drifts about a kilometer per minute. The engineering problem has not changed, only its time constants: an inertial system that is smooth, fast, and wrong in slowly growing ways, a radio position that is noisy, slow, and right on average, and a filter that makes each cover for the other.

``` text
phone IMU (1 Hz) --> mount rotation (given) --> mechanization (Part A) --> L, lambda, h, v, q
                                                       |
GNSS fix (1 Hz) --> residual, lever arm (Part B) --> ESKF: F, Q_d, update, reset (Part B)
                                                       |
x_hat, P every second --> outages, NIS, errors (Part C) --> map matching, guidance, control
```

Project 3 builds that system for a smartphone riding in a car. The consumer at the bottom of the stack (a route-guidance engine snapping you to a lane, a vehicle controller, the perception stack of Project 1 that needs a pose to project its detections) does not want the GNSS fix. It wants a continuous position, velocity, and attitude with a covariance it can believe, including in the tunnel, the parking garage, and the urban canyon where the fix is gone or wrong. Your filter is judged on exactly that: how it behaves when GNSS is withheld, and whether its covariance tells the truth about it.

## Overview {#sec-project3-overview}

You will mechanize a strapdown INS on the curved, rotating Earth from smartphone MEMS data and aid it with loosely coupled GNSS position fixes through a 15-state error-state Kalman filter, following the model of @sec-ins-gnss exactly. The project is worth **25% of the course grade**.

**Learning outcomes.** By the end of the project you should be able to

- implement the local-navigation-frame mechanization of @sec-ins-gnss-navigation-equations-local, with Earth rate, transport rate, Coriolis, and normal gravity, and verify it with tests that a wrong sign cannot pass;
- align an IMU you cannot gyrocompass: level from the accelerometers, take heading from somewhere else;
- derive and implement the error-state model `F`, a process noise `Q_d` traced to an IMU specification, the lever-arm measurement Jacobian `H`, the Joseph-form update, injection, and the reset;
- read a real dataset critically, including a reference solution that is neither truth nor always right;
- evaluate a navigation filter honestly: against withheld measurements during outages, against its own covariance, and with innovation statistics.

## Logistics {#sec-project3-logistics}

**Pace and deadline.** The recommended pace is weeks 12-13, alongside @sec-global-nav, @sec-ins-errors, and @sec-ins-gnss. That is a recommendation, not a deadline: everything is due by the **end of week 16** (@sec-syllabus-course-policies). Early submissions for feedback are welcome.

**Submission.** Submit Project 3 once, on Canvas: a single-column **report PDF** (structure and expectations in @sec-intro-project-guidance), the **source files** of your `ins_gnss` package that you implemented or changed plus any scripts or notebooks you used, and a short `README` listing the exact commands that regenerate every figure and table in the report. Following the course policy (@sec-intro-code-style-guide), upload each file individually rather than as a compressed archive.

**Environment.** From the repository root:

``` bash
uv sync                                                   # install Python and the packages
uv run python scripts/fetch_data.py mems-nav-dataset      # download the data (about 150 MB)
uv run pytest projects/ins_gnss                           # starter tests: support code passes, your stubs skip
uv run ins-gnss                                           # every trial and its status
uv run python -m ins_gnss.run_all                         # run every stage you have implemented so far
```

**AI tools and libraries.** The course policy is in @sec-intro-ai-policy-and-dependencies.

**Reusing book code.** @sec-ins-gnss contains a complete mechanization, error model, and loosely coupled filter running on a simulated drive, and @sec-ins-errors-from-imu-specs turns a datasheet into `Q_d`. You may adapt any of it, with attribution: cite the section in a code comment and in the report. Grading puts its weight on what the book cannot do for you: the evidence that your signs and Jacobians are right, the noise model you can defend, the behavior on real data, and an honest account of consistency. A copied filter that runs earns little; one you can test, tune, and break on purpose earns a lot.

## Dataset {#sec-project3-data}

The project uses the MEMS navigation dataset [@MemsNavDataset]: an Android phone in a car, logging its IMU and GNSS receiver on drives around Philadelphia, to the New Jersey shore, and to Long Island, plus a `baseline/` reference solution for every trial. It is the instructor's own dataset. Download it once:

``` bash
uv run python scripts/fetch_data.py mems-nav-dataset
```

This places 17 trials in `data/mems-nav-dataset/` (`input/`, `baseline/`, `manifest.json`). The starter tools find it automatically; set `ADVNAV_DATA_DIR` to the folder containing `mems-nav-dataset/` if you keep it elsewhere. The facts below were each checked on the files, and several of them are not what you would assume.

| Quantity | What the files contain | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Rate | Every row is one second apart, **the IMU included**; timestamps are whole UTC seconds | Propagate each 1 s interval with the average of its two bounding IMU samples (`run_all` does) |
| IMU axes | The phone's Android sensor axes: $x$ right, $y$ toward the top of the screen, $z$ out of the screen. The accelerometer reads specific force ($+9.8$ m/s$^2$ on the axis pointing up at rest); the gyro output looks bias-compensated by the phone (parked, it averages a few to 60 deg/h per axis, with 0.01-0.09 deg/s of noise per sample) | Rotate to vehicle forward-right-down axes with `estimate_mount_rotation` and `rotate_imu_samples` |
| Mounting | In the recommended trials the phone stands upright in a mount facing the driver, so vehicle forward $\approx -z$, right $\approx +x$, down $\approx -y$, with yaw offsets up to 17 degrees. In four 2025 trials (June 18, June 27, July 4) the phone lies flat or nearly so | The estimated mount rotation handles each trial; check it with `uv run ins-gnss --trial NAME` |
| GNSS | One position fix per second (latitude and longitude in degrees, altitude), plus speed, course over ground (`bearing`, clockwise from north), and the receiver's accuracy estimates | `GNSSSample` carries all of them; `gnss_position_covariance` builds a starting $\mathbf{R}$ from the accuracies |
| Height | Height above the **WGS-84 ellipsoid**: at the shore on the Long Island and Jersey Shore trips the lowest fixes read $-33$ to $-49$ m, where the geoid lies about 33 m below the ellipsoid (@sec-frames-earth-frames) | Use it as $h$ directly |
| Baseline | A GNSS-aided strapdown solution, **not truth**. Its rows are labelled 1 s early relative to the fixes they follow (GitHub issue #5); it has a start-up transient, it diverges by kilometers in some GNSS gaps, its height sits 2-14 m off the GNSS height, and its attitude columns are not in the book's convention | The loader adds `BASELINE_TIME_OFFSET_S` (1 s); compare horizontal position only, where `reference_valid_mask` says the baseline agrees with GNSS. Never fuse it |
| Phone orientation | The phone's own orientation (`qw`...`qz`): gravity is right, heading is not (tens of degrees off, often more) | Sanity checks only, never a measurement; it is in `trial.auxiliary` with the barometer and magnetometer |

Two of these deserve a sentence more. **Time.** The old loader measured the input and the baseline from their own first rows, which are one second apart, and the baseline is labelled a further second early; together that put the "truth" 2 s (about 45 m at highway speed) away from the fixes it was computed from. The loader now uses one epoch, the first input timestamp, and `load_mems_nav_trial(..., baseline_time_offset_s=...)` exposes the correction; with it, the baseline agrees with GNSS to a median of 0.4-0.8 m. **Attitude.** In phone axes the upright phone has a Z-Y-X pitch near $-90°$, gimbal lock, which is one reason to work in vehicle axes. Compare attitudes with `attitude_error` (the rotation vector of $\mathbf{C}_\text{true}\hat{\mathbf{C}}^T$), never by subtracting Euler angles. The one attitude yardstick this dataset offers is the GNSS course: driving straight at speed, the vehicle's yaw should equal it (`heading_error_vs_course`).

Not every trial is usable. `recommended_trials()` returns the five vetted ones, and `TRIAL_NOTES` explains every trial's status:

| Status | Trials | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Recommended | `2023-08-06_144805`, `2023-08-09_163741`, `2025-03-01_164639`, `2025-07-31_23-36-03`, `2025-08-03_18-15-59` | 0.7-4.1 h each, at most two GNSS gaps of 7 s or less, the phone stays in its mount while driving, the baseline agrees with GNSS |
| Caution | the nine others | GNSS gaps after which the baseline jumps up to 6.5 km, a phone moved mid-trial, stale fixes, a flat mount |
| Excluded | `2024-06-20_165550`, `2025-06-11_20-34-24`, `2025-06-14_21-17-02` | a 145 km baseline jump; 443 IMU samples in 27 minutes; fixes every 5 s with 2 km jumps and a baseline 7 km off |

Repeated fixes exist too: most are a parked receiver holding its position, which is fine, but a few dozen in `2025-06-27_11-54-35` repeat while the car moves. `repeated_fix_mask` flags those and `run_all` skips them.

Load a trial with:

``` python
from ins_gnss.datasets import estimate_mount_rotation, load_mems_nav_trial, recommended_trials, rotate_imu_samples

name = recommended_trials()[1]                      # 2023-08-09_163741, the short one
trial = load_mems_nav_trial(None, name)             # finds data/mems-nav-dataset
C_pv = estimate_mount_rotation(trial.imu_samples, trial.gnss_samples)
imu = rotate_imu_samples(trial.imu_samples, C_pv)   # vehicle forward-right-down axes
fix = trial.gnss_samples[0]
print(fix.horizontal_accuracy_m, fix.velocity_ne_mps(), trial.reference_states[0].time_s)
```

What you write, with the signatures the tests and `run_all` call:

``` python
mechanize(state, accel_mps2, gyro_rps, dt_s)               # -> NavState            (Part A)
coarse_alignment(mean_specific_force_b, yaw_rad)            # -> q_b^n               (Part A)
error_state_jacobian(state, specific_force_b)               # -> F, 15 x 15          (Part B)
discrete_process_noise(state, noise, dt_s)                  # -> Q_d, 15 x 15        (Part B)
gnss_position_residual(state, gnss, lever_arm_b)            # -> (nu, H)             (Part B)
joseph_update(P, nu, H, R)                                  # -> (delta_x, P_plus, nis)
inject_error_state(state, delta_x)                          # -> NavState
reset_covariance(P, delta_theta)                            # -> P
gnss_velocity_residual(state, gnss, lever_arm_b, gyro_rps)  # -> (nu, H), only for the velocity extension
```

Their docstrings are the detailed contract. Keep those signatures stable; add helpers, keyword-only options, and modules freely. `INSGNSSFilter` strings them together: `flt.predict(accel_mps2, gyro_rps, dt_s)` mechanizes the nominal state and propagates `flt.P` with `F_d = I + F dt` and your `Q_d`; `flt.update_gnss_position(gnss, R=None, *, gate=None)` computes your residual, runs your update, injects, resets, and appends an `InnovationRecord` (with the NIS) to `flt.innovations`. It is a plain dataclass, so give it whatever extra attributes you need.

The tests of your deliverables skip with a "not implemented yet" message until you write the corresponding function, then start checking it, so `uv run pytest projects/ins_gnss` is a quick sanity check as you go. They are strict about signs: a perfect IMU at rest at 42° N must stay at rest for a minute, a perfect IMU driving east must hold its velocity (Coriolis and transport rate), `F` must match a finite-difference Jacobian of *your* `mechanize`, `H` with a lever arm must match finite differences of *your* residual, and the reset must match the exact attitude reset. They do not check whether your filter is any good on the real data. `uv run python -m ins_gnss.run_all` runs whatever you have implemented on the recommended trials and reports the rest as not implemented; its `TUNING` block is where your values go.

## System Model {#sec-project3-system-model}

The model is the one of @sec-ins-gnss, written once more so there is no doubt about what is graded. The nominal state is

$$
\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \left[\hat L,\ \hat\lambda,\ \hat h,\ \hat{\mathbf{v}}^n,\ \hat{\mathbf{q}}_b^n,\ \hat{\mathbf{b}}_a,\ \hat{\mathbf{b}}_g\right],
$$

with the NED navigation frame, the vehicle forward-right-down body frame, and corrected measurements $\hat{\mathbf{f}}^b = \tilde{\mathbf{f}}^b - \hat{\mathbf{b}}_a$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_{ib}^b = \tilde{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_{ib}^b - \hat{\mathbf{b}}_g$.

**Mechanization** (@sec-ins-gnss-navigation-equations-local, Groves Section 5.4 [@groves]). Over a step $\tau$: attitude first, $\hat{\mathbf{q}}(+) = \mathbf{q}(-\boldsymbol{\omega}_{in}^n\tau) \otimes \hat{\mathbf{q}}(-) \otimes \mathbf{q}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\omega}}_{ib}^b\tau)$ with exact rotation-vector quaternions and $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{in}^n = \boldsymbol{\omega}_{ie}^n + \boldsymbol{\omega}_{en}^n$; then velocity,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{f}^n &= \tfrac12\left(\mathbf{C}_b^n(-) + \mathbf{C}_b^n(+)\right)\hat{\mathbf{f}}^b,\\
\mathbf{v}^n(+) &= \mathbf{v}^n(-) + \left[\mathbf{f}^n + \mathbf{g}^n(L, h) - \left(\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{en}^n + 2\boldsymbol{\Omega}_{ie}^n\right)\mathbf{v}^n(-)\right]\tau;
\end{aligned}
$$

then position, trapezoidally, with $R_M$ and $R_N$ the meridian and prime-vertical radii (Groves calls them $R_N$ and $R_E$). Gravity is Somigliana normal gravity with the free-air correction of @sec-ins-gnss-gravity, positive down (`compute_gravity`; 9.7803 m/s$^2$ on the equator, 9.8322 m/s$^2$ at the poles).

**Error state** (@sec-ins-gnss-error-state-formulation), true minus estimate:

$$
\delta\mathbf{x} = \left[\delta\mathbf{p},\ \delta\mathbf{v},\ \delta\boldsymbol{\theta},\ \delta\mathbf{b}_a,\ \delta\mathbf{b}_g\right],
$$

with the position error in NED meters,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta p_N &= (R_M + h)\,\delta L,\\
\delta p_E &= (R_N + h)\cos L\,\delta\lambda,\\
\delta p_D &= -\delta h,
\end{aligned}
$$

with the attitude error in the navigation frame, $\mathbf{C}_b^n = (\mathbf{I} + [\delta\boldsymbol{\theta}]_\times)\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n$. Biases come in the order accelerometer, then gyro, everywhere. The short-horizon MEMS error model neglects the Earth-rate, transport-rate, and gravity-gradient couplings, which matter over tens of minutes of unaided navigation, not over the seconds between fixes or the minutes of an outage, for a sensor whose noise and bias instability swamp Earth rate (@sec-ins-gnss-error-state-formulation):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta\dot{\mathbf{p}} &= \delta\mathbf{v},\\
\delta\dot{\mathbf{v}} &= -[\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\hat{\mathbf{f}}^b]_\times\,\delta\boldsymbol{\theta} - \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\,\delta\mathbf{b}_a + \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\mathbf{w}_a,\\
\delta\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}} &= -\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\,\delta\mathbf{b}_g + \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\mathbf{w}_g,\\
\delta\dot{\mathbf{b}}_a &= \mathbf{w}_{ba},\\
\delta\dot{\mathbf{b}}_g &= \mathbf{w}_{bg}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Discretize with $\mathbf{F}_d \approx \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{F}\tau$ and $\mathbf{Q}_d \approx \mathbf{G}\mathbf{Q}_c\mathbf{G}^T\tau$ (or Van Loan, @sec-kf-process-noise), $\mathbf{Q}_c$ built from `IMUNoise`: velocity random walk $N_a$, angle random walk $N_g$, and the bias random walks.

**GNSS position** (@sec-ins-gnss-loose-gnss-measurement, @sec-ins-gnss-lever-arm-timing). The fix, converted to NED meters relative to the nominal IMU position, is predicted as $\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b$ for an antenna at lever arm $\boldsymbol{\ell}^b$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\boldsymbol{\nu} &= \mathbf{z} - \hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b,\\
\mathbf{H} &= \left[\mathbf{I}_3,\ \mathbf{0},\ -[\hat{\mathbf{C}}_b^n\boldsymbol{\ell}^b]_\times,\ \mathbf{0},\ \mathbf{0}\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

The phone's antenna and IMU are centimeters apart, so the honest lever arm here is zero; your code must still handle a nonzero one (the tests use one). Update with the Joseph form, inject (position back through the radii, $\hat{\mathbf{q}} \leftarrow \delta\mathbf{q}(\delta\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}) \otimes \hat{\mathbf{q}}$), and reset with $\mathbf{G} = \operatorname{blkdiag}(\mathbf{I}, \mathbf{I}, \mathbf{I} + [\tfrac12\delta\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}]_\times, \mathbf{I}, \mathbf{I})$ (@eq-ekf-reset-jacobian).

## Part A: Mechanization and Alignment {#sec-project3-part-curved-earth}

**Goal.** A strapdown INS you can trust before any filter touches it.

1.  Implement `mechanize`. Pass the provided tests, then add one of your own that exercises something they do not (a north-going drive, a climb, a constant turn) and explain what bug it would catch.
2.  Implement `coarse_alignment` (@sec-ins-gnss-alignment). `run_all` levels from the samples of the minute before the car leaves (or, if a log starts on the move, from the first 10 s with the GNSS-derived acceleration removed) and takes heading from the GNSS course at departure. Explain why heading cannot come from the gyros here, and estimate the tilt error your leveling leaves (an accelerometer bias $b_a$ looks like a tilt of $b_a/g$).
3.  Real-data sanity checks, all printed by `run_all`: free-inertial navigation for 60 s after departure, scored against GNSS, and the "parked check" (60 s of free inertial on a quiet parked stretch, where any motion is error). Plot the error growth and relate it to the bias and noise sizes of @sec-ins-errors-why-bias-dominates: which term dominates after 10 s, after 60 s?
4.  Report the mount rotation of each trial and how you checked it. Show, with numbers, what goes wrong if you skip it and run the filter on phone axes.

Expect free-inertial errors to be humbling: up to tens of meters after ten seconds, hundreds of meters to kilometers after a minute. That is what a smartphone IMU is, not a bug, but a velocity that runs away in the first second *is* a bug.

## Part B: The Error-State Filter {#sec-project3-part-b-error}

**Goal.** A loosely coupled ESKF whose every matrix you can defend.

1.  Implement `error_state_jacobian` and `discrete_process_noise`. Show in the report the numerical check of `F` against your mechanization (the test does it; plot or tabulate the largest discrepancies and explain the ones the short-horizon model neglects).
2.  Build `IMUNoise` from a specification, not from thin air. Start from a consumer MEMS datasheet and the grade table of @sec-ins-errors-imu-grades, convert units as in @sec-ins-errors-from-imu-specs, and then argue how much to inflate it: these samples are 1 Hz, so the process noise must also cover what a once-per-second sample misses (vibration, rate changes within the second, road grade). Inflation is allowed; unexplained inflation is not.
3.  Implement `gnss_position_residual`, `joseph_update`, `inject_error_state`, and `reset_covariance`. Choose $\mathbf{R}$: `gnss_position_covariance` starts from the receiver's own accuracy estimates (Android reports a 68% horizontal radius), which you may scale; justify the choice with the NIS.
4.  Decide whether to gate innovations (`gate=` in `update_gnss_position`; the 99.9% point for 3 degrees of freedom is 16.27) and show what it rejects.
5.  Plot, for at least one trial, the position, velocity, attitude, and bias standard deviations against time, and the estimated biases. Say which states are observable when, with reference to @sec-ins-errors-observability-loose-ins: when does yaw become observable, and what does the yaw sigma do on a long straight?

## Part C: Evaluation {#sec-project3-part-c-performance}

**Goal.** Show what GNSS aiding buys, what the IMU buys when GNSS is gone, and whether the filter knows how well it is doing. Follow @sec-project3-evaluation-protocol on all five recommended trials.

1.  **GNSS only versus loose INS/GNSS.** Compare both against the valid reference. Do not be surprised if GNSS only wins by a few decimeters to a meter: the reference is a GNSS-aided solution that hugs the fixes, so this comparison measures closeness to GNSS more than closeness to truth. Explain that, and say what the comparison *can* show (smoothness, velocity, attitude, behavior at stops).
2.  **Scheduled outages** of 10, 30, 60, and 120 s, scored against the withheld fixes: error against time with the filter's 3-sigma envelope, next to the constant-velocity extrapolation a receiver would do on its own. Expect the INS to win by a factor of two to four at 30-60 s, and not always: say when and why it loses.
3.  **Consistency.** NIS against the chi-square bounds (@sec-kf-consistency), the fraction of outage errors inside 1 and 3 sigma, and a diagnosis. A mean NIS far above 3 means the filter is overconfident; far below means underconfident, or GNSS errors that are correlated in time (they are). Then tune and show the effect.
4.  **Heading.** The yaw-minus-course statistics on straight driving, and what they say about alignment and the mount rotation.

## Extensions {#sec-project3-extensions}

Pick one or two, and evaluate them with the same protocol as the baseline filter.

- **RTS smoothing through outages.** Run a Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother over the error-state filter (store the priors, posteriors, and transition matrices) and show how much of each outage error it removes once GNSS returns.
- **Horizontal velocity aiding.** Implement `gnss_velocity_residual` and turn on `use_velocity_aiding`; use `gnss_velocity_covariance` (speed and course accuracies propagated through @sec-ins-gnss-loose-gnss-measurement) as a starting $\mathbf{R}$. Skip it below a few meters per second, where course is noise.
- **Vehicle constraints.** Non-holonomic pseudo-measurements (zero lateral and vertical velocity in the vehicle frame) and zero-velocity updates when parked. These need the mount rotation to be right, and they change outage performance more than anything else on this list.
- **Barometer altitude.** `trial.auxiliary` holds pressure and Android's relative altitude; model the barometer's bias and fuse it in the vertical channel, which is where loosely coupled GNSS is weakest.
- **Tight coupling.** Pseudoranges and Doppler instead of positions (@sec-adv-gnss-tight-coupling). This dataset has no raw GNSS measurements; Android's GnssLogger app records them, so this extension means collecting your own data. Talk to the instructor first.

## Evaluation Protocol {#sec-project3-evaluation-protocol}

Everyone measures the same way, so results can be compared. `ins_gnss.evaluation` implements each step and `run_all` applies them.

1.  **Trials.** All five of `recommended_trials()`. Others are optional; say which and quote their `TRIAL_NOTES`.
2.  **Run window.** The filter starts at departure (the first fix after which the speed stays above 5 m/s for 5 s) and stops 30 s after the last fix faster than 5 m/s, as `run_all.prepare_trial` does; justify any change.
3.  **Errors against the reference.** At the reference timestamps where `reference_valid_mask` holds (a fix within 0.5 s that agrees to 10 m), with the estimate *interpolated* to those times (`position_error_ned`): horizontal RMSE, median, 95th percentile, and maximum (`error_summary`). Do the same for GNSS only (`gnss_only_track`). Vertical errors against the baseline are unreliable; report them with that caveat or not at all.
4.  **Outages.** Schedule the outage windows with

    ``` python
    schedule_outages(trial.gnss_samples, (10, 30, 60, 120),
                     first_start_s=start + 300, spacing_s=400)
    ```

    The windows begin while moving, at least 90% of their seconds have a fix, and the filter gets 280 s or more to reconverge between them. Withhold those fixes from the filter, score against them (`outage_errors`), and compare with `constant_velocity_outage_errors`. Report the median and maximum error at 10, 30, 60, and 120 s into the outages, and the fraction inside the 3-sigma envelope $3\sqrt{P_{NN} + P_{EE}}$.
5.  **Consistency.** Every NIS with the single-sample 95% interval for 3 degrees of freedom, $[0.22, 9.35]$ (`chi2_interval(3)`), the fraction inside, and the mean NIS with its averaged bounds (optimistic, because GNSS errors are correlated in time).
6.  **Heading.** `heading_error_vs_course` above 8 m/s: median and median absolute deviation.
7.  **Cost.** Runtime per trial on stated hardware.

2.  Tests beyond the provided ones: at least the extra mechanization test of Part A and a test for your extension.
3.  The report PDF, with: the data checks you made and how; the mount rotation and alignment; the mechanization and its verification; `F`, `Q_d` (with the datasheet it came from and every inflation factor), `H`, $\mathbf{R}$, and the gate; the evaluation of @sec-project3-evaluation-protocol with the required figures; the consistency diagnosis and tuning; the extension; and a discussion of failure modes.

Keep the report concise and technical. A covariance plot with an honest sentence under it beats three pages on the history of the gyroscope.

## Suggested Milestones {#sec-project3-suggested-milestones}

1.  Load a recommended trial, plot GNSS, run `uv run ins-gnss --trial NAME`, and look at the mount rotation.
2.  Write `mechanize` and `coarse_alignment`; pass their tests; run the Part A checks in `run_all`.
3.  Write `F` and `Q_d`; pass the numerical-Jacobian test.
4.  Write the residual, update, injection, and reset; pass the synthetic-drive consistency test.
5.  Run `run_all` on one short trial, read the plots, tune, then run all five.
6.  Run the outage study, diagnose consistency, tune again (and say what you changed).
7.  Do the extension, then write the report around the evidence.
